title: LIDAR with Optically Amplified Thermal Light
authors: Darren Ming Zhi Koh, Peng Kian Tan, Christian Kurtsiefer
abstract: Thermal light exhibits intensity fluctuations or photon bunching that has been used as a source of entropy or temporally correlated light. However, its low spectral density limits its use in practical applications like LIDAR. One method of remedying this is optical amplification to boost its brightness. In this paper, we show that the normalized second order coherence function $g^{(2)}(τ)$ of a thermal light source is preserved after amplification. We then use amplified thermal light to demonstrate a LIDAR raster scan of a building at 1.3 km with a depth resolution of 2 cm.
summary: This paper demonstrates that amplified thermal light can be effectively used for long-range LIDAR applications. The authors prove that the key quantum signature, the second-order coherence function g^(2)(τ), remains intact after optical amplification. This allowed them to successfully map a building at 1.3 km with high depth resolution.
main_problem: The primary challenge is utilizing thermal light for practical applications like LIDAR, which is limited by the low spectral density of the light source.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a LIDAR raster scan of a building at 1.3 km with a depth resolution of 2 cm using amplified thermal light.
method: The experiment involved characterizing the normalized second-order coherence function, g^(2)(τ), of amplified thermal light and using this property to measure distances via time-of-flight measurements.
model_or_system: The system uses thermal light, which is amplified (e.g., via EDFA) to boost brightness. The coherence properties are analyzed using the normalized second-order coherence function, g^(2)(τ), which is shown to be preserved after amplification.
key_observables: Normalized second-order coherence function, g^(2)(τ); distance (d) derived from the time delay (τ_d = 2d/c).
important_parameters: 1.3 km range; 2 cm depth resolution; 1550 nm wavelength; 60 s integration time.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the amplified spontaneous emission (ASE) is thermal light with a broadband spectrum, and that the preservation of g^(2)(τ) holds true after amplification.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares brightness of thermal sources; Figure 2 shows the experimental setup; Figure 3 compares optical spectra and g^(2)(τ) at different amplification stages (A-D); Figure 4 shows the raster scan result; Figure 5 confirms distance calculation using g^(2)(τ_d) peaks.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical basis by showing that g^(2)(τ) is preserved during optical amplification. It then details the experimental setup and measurements, culminating in the successful demonstration of the LIDAR scan.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical application of quantum light sources (thermal light) by overcoming fundamental limitations (low spectral density) through amplification, which is a key topic in quantum optics and quantum sensing.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Comparison of brightness and spectral widths of dif- ferent thermal light sources. Light sources in the green region have unresolvable intensity fluctuations. Light sources in the purple region are dimmer than the ASE of an optical ampli- fier, assuming a uniform ASE spectral density of 1 µW/nm. Amplifiable light sources with resolvable coherence time are in the white region. Microsphere suspension (MS) and ro- tating ground glass (RGG) are pseudothermal light sources whose intensity fluctuation arise from scattering light through a time-varying dispersive medium. As such, their coherence time do not depend on their spectral width. SLD: superlumi- nescent diode.
